summary.one_line: A fast-growing Jaipur power-distribution EPC contractor whose profits have not yet turned into cash. It has no real moat and depends almost entirely on state discoms. Most of the new money will fund receivables and retention money, not new capacity. Worth tracking after listing, not applying to today.
bull_points: Revenue from operations rose from Rs 209.58 cr in FY24 to Rs 503.57 cr in FY26. Over the same period EBITDA margin widened from 11.31% to 14.07% and PAT went from Rs 13.98 cr to Rs 41.43 cr (S1).

Order visibility is real. At 31 July 2026 there were 18 ongoing projects worth Rs 2,036.65 cr, with Rs 916.55 cr of work still to be executed (S1, S6). Every order comes from government utilities, many of them funded by the World Bank or by Government of India schemes (S1, S6).
Litigation is light. The company has no criminal cases and no regulatory actions against it. There are two civil writ petitions it filed itself, plus four tax cases totalling Rs 44.62 lakh (S1).

The balance sheet was repaired before the IPO. A Rs 40 cr pre-IPO placement at Rs 165 helped bring debt-to-equity down from 1.44x in FY25 to 0.73x in FY26 (S1). CRISIL now rates the company BBB+/Stable, having rated it BB- earlier (S20).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in all three years: Rs -3.34 cr, Rs -76.54 cr and Rs -9.65 cr. Over the same years the company reported about Rs 82.9 cr of cumulative PAT (S1, S11).
Customer concentration is extreme. The top five clients gave 96.87% of FY26 revenue and the single largest gave 31.44% (S1). Government utilities make up 100% of the order book (S6).

Apart from issue expenses, the fresh money goes only to working capital (Rs 90 cr) and general corporate purposes (S1, S9). It pays for receivables and retention money, not for any capability that would build a moat. The Rs 32.38 cr OFS goes to the selling shareholders (S4).

Governance flags: from 1 April 2025 the promoter couple's monthly pay ceiling was tripled from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 30 lakh (S7). The company's credit rating was cut in FY22 and it was tagged 'Issuer Not Cooperating' (S1, S27).
watch_points: Whether operating cash flow turns positive in the first two reported half-years after listing. The FY27 plan assumes receivable days fall from 83 to 75 and payable days from 91 to 60 (S9).
New order wins outside RDSS. RDSS's original funding window covered FY22 to FY26 (S26). The order book's cover of FY26 EPC revenue has already fallen from 2.08x in FY24 to 1.41x (S1).
The outcome of the Rajasthan High Court writ over a Rs 3.60 cr recovery demand from JVVNL. The next hearing is on 16 November 2026 (S12).
Final category-wise subscription on 25 September 2026. The QIB book matters most, because the anchor book was filled by six little-known funds and not by domestic mutual funds (S17, S18).

reasoning: The growth has not yet produced cash. Over FY24 to FY26 the company reported about Rs 82.9 cr of PAT but used about Rs 89.5 cr in operations (S1, S11). Working capital rose from Rs 73.35 cr to Rs 255.63 cr, about 51% of revenue (S11). Until a listed half-year shows profits turning into cash, the headline 35.44% RoNW (S1) overstates what shareholders actually earn.

The fresh issue funds working capital, not a moat. Rs 90 cr goes to incremental working capital, the rest to general corporate purposes and issue costs (S1). The FY27 plan needs net working capital of Rs 415.97 cr, up from Rs 255.63 cr (S9). The IPO pays for the next round of receivables and retention money. It does not buy new capability or pricing power.

There is no real competitive moat. The company wins work in L1-style tenders run by state discoms: it won 8 of the 28 bids it entered in FY26 (S6). It has 182 employees, of whom 65 are engineers or technicians (S21), and describes itself as asset-light (S1). Larger EPC players such as KEC and Kalpataru bid for the same work (S28). The one real advantage is a record of qualifying for utility tenders, and competitors can replicate that.

Its fortunes are tied to one policy cycle and a handful of clients. The top five customers gave 96.87% of FY26 revenue (S1). The five largest projects make up 69.72% of the unexecuted order book, and the single biggest, the Sikar circle segregation project, is 24.58% (S6). RDSS was sanctioned for FY22 to FY26 (S26). If follow-on discom spending slows, revenue can fall quickly.

Governance is not alarming, but it is not clean either. RPTs are small, at 3.96% of FY26 revenue (S27). Against that, the promoter couple's pay ceiling was tripled just before listing (S7). The company had a CARE BB- 'Issuer Not Cooperating' history (S27) and pending ROC Jaipur adjudication over delayed filings (S5). Promoter selling shareholders are exiting part of their holdings acquired at Rs 4.30 to Rs 14.80 a share (S1).

What would change the call: a positive operating cash flow print, receivable and retention days falling towards the FY27 plan, and new non-RDSS orders that lift the order book back above 2x revenue. Any of these would support moving from 'track' to 'invest' (S1, S9).

blocks.text: Swastika Infra is a Jaipur-based engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor for power transmission and distribution. Its projects cover underground cabling, gas- and air-insulated substations and grid substations, rural and urban electrification, street lighting and renewable-energy electrical works, all done on a turnkey basis from supply through erection, testing and commissioning (S1). In practice most of the work is at distribution voltages: underground and overhead lines up to 33 kV (S14). This is the unglamorous last-mile grid build-out that state discoms put out to tender.

The business goes back to M/s Swastika Electricals & Fertilizers, a partnership that promoter Babulal Gupta set up in 1969 (S1). It moved from trading electrical goods into EPC execution in 2012 (S14) and became a private limited company in August 2019 (S1, S16). It became a public limited company in January 2025 (S16). The DRHP was filed with SEBI on 1 April 2025 (S3) and the RHP on 17 September 2026 (S2).

At the RHP date the company had completed 36 power-distribution projects across six states and had 18 ongoing projects, also across six states (S1). Completed work includes about 18,579 km of distribution lines, with a completed contract value of Rs 76,467 lakh, or about Rs 765 cr (S4, S20, S21). Headcount is small: 182 employees at 31 July 2026, of whom 65 are engineers or technicians (S21, S22). Field labour and specialised work are therefore largely subcontracted, and the RHP-based reviews list subcontractor dependence as a risk (S24).

In one sentence: Swastika wins state-utility tenders for distribution-network works, buys cables, transformers and switchgear, deploys subcontracted crews under its own project engineers, and is paid in milestones. A slice of each bill is held back as retention money until the defect-liability period ends. This model explains both the growth and the cash drain (S1, S9).

subsections.title: How revenue is earned: segments, customers and concentration

blocks.text: The company reports two segments: EPC Power Projects, and a small sale-of-products line (trading of power cables and electrical products). EPC's share has risen from 90% of revenue in FY24 to 97% in FY26 (S1, S16). The customers are almost all government. Projects for government utilities brought in Rs 487.82 cr, or 96.87% of FY26 revenue, up from 89.84% in FY24 (S6).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (share of revenue from operations) (S1)

blocks.text: The named customer list is a roll-call of state utilities: WBSEDCL (West Bengal), MGVCL (Gujarat), APDCL (Assam), Goa Electricity Department, HPSEBL (Himachal), UHBVN (Haryana), JVVNL and AVVNL (Rajasthan discoms), UPCL (Uttarakhand), MSEDCL (Maharashtra) and RRVPNL (Rajasthan transmission) (S1). Concentration in the single largest customer has come down, from 61% in FY24 to 31% in FY26. Even so, the top five still provide almost all revenue, and the company can never have more than a handful of large contracts running at once (S1).

Pricing is set by the tender. Contracts are won by competitive bidding after meeting pre-qualification criteria, and the RHP lists this as a top-10 risk factor (S1). In FY26 the company won 8 of the 28 bids it entered, after 2 of 10 in FY25 and 6 of 16 in FY24 (S6). A win rate of about 20-40% is typical of commodity tendering and points to no pricing power.

subsections.title: Order book, operations and supply chain

blocks.text: At 31 July 2026 the 18 ongoing projects had an aggregate order value of Rs 2,036.65 cr, of which Rs 916.55 cr was still to be executed (S1, S6). The order book at financial year-end was Rs 391.39 cr in FY24, Rs 650.23 cr in FY25 and Rs 687.44 cr in FY26. Over the same years order-book cover fell from 2.08x to 1.92x to 1.41x of EPC revenue (S1, S11). Revenue grew faster than orders were replenished.

blocks.caption: Five largest projects by unexecuted value, 31 July 2026 (S6)

blocks.text: The operating model is asset-light. The company leases project-specific equipment instead of owning a large plant, and reported a fixed-asset turnover of 70.72x in FY26 (S5, S20). The price of that model is working capital. At FY26 the balance sheet carried Rs 114.98 cr of trade receivables, Rs 160.02 cr of retention money held by clients, Rs 41.47 cr of unbilled revenue and Rs 35.55 cr of margin money behind bank guarantees (S9). Contingent liabilities, mostly bank guarantees given to government clients, stood at Rs 272.68 cr (S5, S15).

Suppliers are not named in any source we could open, and the abridged prospectus gives no supplier-concentration figure (S1). The debt structure shows how procurement is financed. At 31 July 2026, Rs 73.26 cr of the Rs 128.34 cr of borrowings, or 57%, was channel finance and TReDS: supplier-invoice discounting through MYND Solution, RXIL, RBL Bank, A.TREDS and Standard Chartered (S10). In effect, cable and equipment purchases are paid through fintech and bank discounting lines while the company waits to be paid by discoms.

subsections.title: Market size and the policy engine behind it

blocks.text: The RHP's industry chapter frames demand through consumption. Citing the CEA, it gives India's power consumption as 1,440.31 TWh in FY23, about 1,500 TWh in 2023, and projected 2030 demand of 2,060-2,699 TWh; with T&D losses included, utility-level demand is 2,039-2,454 TWh (S1). These are national demand figures. They are not the addressable market for 33 kV distribution EPC, and the prospectus does not give a clean market-size number for Swastika's niche (S1).

The spending that actually drives Swastika's order book is the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS). It has an outlay of Rs 3,03,758 cr over FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26, including Rs 97,631 cr of central gross budgetary support (S13, S26). Sanctions included Rs 1,21,778 cr for loss-reduction infrastructure, the category Swastika's cabling, feeder-segregation and substation work falls into, alongside Rs 1,30,474 cr for smart metering (S13). The company explicitly presents itself as a beneficiary of RDSS (S14).

RDSS's sanctioned window was FY22-FY26 (S26). Much of the FY24-FY26 surge in distribution EPC tenders ties to that scheme, so its extension or successor, and discoms' ability to fund their share, decide whether FY27-FY28 orders keep pace. The order-book cover ratio has already slipped from 2.08x to 1.41x (S1).

subsections.title: Competitors and whether there is a moat

blocks.text: The offer document names Rajesh Power Services and Vikran Engineering as its listed peers (S28). Both are distribution and transmission EPC contractors that also depend on utility tenders. Much larger diversified EPC firms such as KEC International and Kalpataru also bid for the same kind of utility work (S28). Below them sits a long tail of unlisted regional electrical contractors in every state, so competition is on price in each tender (S1).

items: No import-substitution, proprietary-technology or regulatory-licence barrier is claimed. The five strengths the RHP lists are execution capability, a scalable model, financial performance, asset-light operations and experienced leadership (S1). These are generic to EPC prospectuses.
No market-share claim appears in the material we could access (S1).

The real, if modest, advantage is pre-qualification. The company has a record of 36 completed utility projects (S1), which lets it bid for larger tenders. The RHP-based reviews note it may need joint ventures to qualify for bigger ones (S14).
The RHP itself lists as a risk that the company 'may not be able to adequately protect our intellectual property' (S1). For a tender contractor, that mainly means the brand.

blocks.text: Plain answer: there is no durable moat. Swastika is a competent, fast-growing regional tender contractor. Its edge is execution record and utility relationships, which peers can replicate, and its bid win rate (8 of 28 in FY26) shows it is a price-taker (S6).

subsections.title: Where Swastika sits within the peer set

blocks.text: At about Rs 504 cr of FY26 revenue (S1), Swastika is small next to diversified EPC players. Its margin profile is respectable for distribution work: EBITDA margin was 14.07% in FY26, up from 11.31% in FY24 (S1). Part of that improvement comes from the shift away from low-margin product trading, which fell from 10% of revenue to 3% (S1). The rest reflects operating leverage on a thin fixed-cost base.

Management's stated strategy is to widen the geographic footprint, focus on high-value EPC projects and diversify into allied infrastructure (S1). In FY26 the company entered power transmission and renewable-energy evacuation work, and won its largest single distribution order, from AVVNL (S14). The Pugal solar park evacuation project, now the second-largest in the order book, is the first sign of that diversification (S6).

Geographic spread is real but shallow. Past projects span Assam, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat (S1), yet Rajasthan projects account for over 40% of the unexecuted order book (S6).

blocks.caption: Restated financials (Rs cr; converted from Rs lakh in the abridged prospectus) (S1)

blocks.text: The growth is steep and real on the P&L. Revenue from operations rose 67% in FY25 and 44% in FY26. PAT almost tripled in two years, from Rs 13.98 cr to Rs 41.43 cr (S1). On a longer view, total income was only about Rs 59.5 cr in FY22 (S23), so the business has grown roughly eightfold in four years. That growth came almost entirely from winning RDSS-era distribution tenders (S6, S13).

Margins improved every year: EBITDA margin went from 11.31% to 12.51% to 14.07%, and PAT margin from 6.67% to 8.23% (S1). But finance costs more than doubled, from Rs 6.50 cr in FY25 to Rs 14.57 cr in FY26 (S10). That shows how much of the growth is being financed by borrowing against working capital.

subsections.title: Cash flow and working capital: the central red flag

blocks.text: Cumulative restated PAT over FY24-FY26 was about Rs 82.9 cr, while cumulative operating cash flow was about Rs -89.5 cr (S1). None of the three years' profit turned into operating cash. The gap is working capital: the company's own net working-capital figure rose from Rs 73.35 cr (35.0% of revenue) in FY24 to Rs 184.98 cr (52.7%) in FY25 and Rs 255.63 cr (50.8%) in FY26 (S11).

blocks.caption: Working-capital build and FY27 plan (Rs cr) (S9)

blocks.text: Retention money, cash held back by utilities until defect-liability periods expire, is the largest single asset in working capital, at Rs 160.02 cr at FY26 (S9). The FY27 plan assumes receivable days improve from 83 to 75 while retention stays at 120 days. It also assumes supplier credit shrinks sharply, from 91 to 60 payable days (S9). The company is planning to lean less on suppliers, which is why it needs the IPO cash.

Operating cash flow has been negative for three straight years (Rs -3.34 cr, -76.54 cr, -9.65 cr), and the RHP itself lists this among its top-10 risks (S1). A 35% RoNW (S1) means little to shareholders if it stays locked in retention money and receivables with state discoms.

Leverage looks moderate after the pre-IPO placement: debt/equity was 0.73x at FY26, down from 1.44x at FY25 (S1). The fall came from new equity, not from debt repayment. Net worth doubled from Rs 77.02 cr to Rs 156.78 cr, helped by the Rs 40 cr pre-IPO placement at Rs 165 a share and FY26 profit (S1). Share capital rose from Rs 24.75 cr to Rs 27.17 cr, matching the 24.24 lakh placement shares (S1).

blocks.caption: Borrowing mix at 31 July 2026 (Rs cr) (S10)
rows: Cash credit / overdraft (HDFC, ICICI, SBI, Federal)

blocks.text: Borrowings rose again after year-end, from Rs 114.64 cr at FY26 to Rs 128.34 cr at 31 July 2026 (S10). Most of the debt is unsecured (Rs 78.49 cr) and short-term: supplier-finance lines from fintech platforms, at disclosed rates of around 8.5-8.6% (S10). Bank lines carry personal guarantees from the promoters and covenants restricting further borrowing or expansion without lender consent (S10). Off balance sheet, bank guarantees and other contingent liabilities of Rs 272.68 cr at FY26 are about 1.7x net worth (S5, S1).

Does the trend support the growth story? On the P&L, yes. On cash, not yet: every rupee of growth has needed more than a rupee of working capital, financed by supplier discounting and now by IPO equity (S1, S9, S10).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Offer terms (S1, S4, S19)
rows: Opens 23 Sep 2026, closes 25 Sep 2026; anchor bid 22 Sep; allotment 28 Sep; listing 30 Sep (BSE, NSE)
Rs 160.88 cr (86,95,946 shares at upper band)
Rs 128.50 cr (69,45,946 shares); RHP cap Rs 129.00 cr
17,50,000 shares, Rs 32.38 cr at upper band
QIB up to 50%, NII at least 15%, retail at least 35%
Srujan Alpha Capital Advisors LLP, PhillipCapital (India) / MUFG Intime India

blocks.text: The issue has shrunk since the DRHP. The April 2025 DRHP proposed a Rs 200 cr fresh issue and a 19.2 lakh-share OFS, with Rs 145 cr earmarked for working capital (S23). A Rs 40 cr pre-IPO placement of 24,24,242 shares at Rs 165 to 78 allottees was then done, and the fresh issue was cut to Rs 129 cr (S1). Net proceeds of Rs 38.09 cr from that placement have already gone into working capital, and the IPO's working-capital object was reduced to Rs 90 cr (S1, S9).

About Rs 128.5 cr of the Rs 160.88 cr issue, roughly 80%, is fresh money for the company. The remaining Rs 32.38 cr is OFS and goes to the sellers (S4). Promoter holding falls from 76.51% to 57.41%, partly because of the OFS and partly because of dilution from the fresh issue (S4).

blocks.caption: Use of fresh-issue proceeds (S1, S9)
rows: Balance, capped at 25% of gross proceeds (up to about 32.25)
Balance of gross proceeds (not disclosed in sources)

blocks.text: There is no capex and no stated debt repayment. Apart from issue costs, all of the fresh money funds working capital and general corporate purposes (S1). The FY27 working-capital plan needs Rs 415.97 cr of net working capital. It is funded by Rs 112.00 cr of current borrowings, Rs 38.09 cr of net pre-IPO money, Rs 90.00 cr of IPO proceeds and Rs 175.88 cr of internal accruals and existing equity (S9). CRISIL Ratings is the monitoring agency (S9).

For the investor, a working-capital IPO means the new equity mostly finances retention money and receivables with state discoms. The use is legitimate, and without it the company would have to borrow more. But it builds no new capability or entry barrier, so it only earns a return if cash conversion improves (S9, S11).

subsections.title: Offer for sale: who is selling and at what cost

blocks.caption: Selling shareholders and weighted average cost of acquisition (S1)

blocks.text: The OFS is small, at about 20% of the issue (S4), and all of it goes to the sellers. Promoters account for 12.03 lakh of the 17.5 lakh shares sold (S1). All sellers bought at Rs 4.30 to Rs 14.80 a share, against a Rs 185 cap (S1). Biren Parnami, Manoj Modi and the Bhartia siblings got their shares from Vinay Gupta in April 2023 at Rs 14.80 (S8). The OFS is modest in size, but it is a partial exit by insiders who entered cheaply, three years before listing.

Over the last three years, the weighted average cost of all shares transacted was Rs 0.89, in a range of Rs 0.00 to Rs 20.00, because gift transfers are counted at zero (S1). The pre-IPO placement at Rs 165 (S1) is the only recent arm's-length equity price below the Rs 175-185 band.

blocks.caption: Promoters and key persons (S1, S7, S8, S21)
rows: B.Com; joined the firm in 1993; 27+ years in EPC and electrical trading

blocks.text: This is a family-run business. Vinay Gupta is Babulal Gupta's son and Ruchira Gupta is Vinay's wife (S7). The board has three family members and three independent directors: Madhvi Sharma, Ajay Gupta and Dileep Kumar Jain (S1). The operating track record belongs to Vinay Gupta, who spent three decades in the family firm. No other listed ventures of the promoters appear in the material we reviewed. Two of the six promoters have only 4-5 years of sector experience (S1).

The promoter shareholding was reshuffled shortly before the IPO. In April 2023 Vinay Gupta transferred 1.19 cr shares at Rs 14.80: 39.6 lakh each to Parnami and Modi, and 19.8 lakh each to Ishaan and Ishita Bhartia (S8). In September 2024 he rebuilt his stake, mainly through a gift of 41.08 lakh shares from his father (S8). Governance roles were formalised on 6 March 2025, when Vinay became MD and Ruchira WTD, and a Nomination and Remuneration Committee was constituted only on 21 March 2025 (S7).

Related-party transactions are listed as a top-10 risk factor (S1). By value they are small and falling: 7.96% of revenue in FY24, 5.14% in FY25 and 3.96% in FY26. They cover salaries, interest, rent, purchases, sales, freight and consumables (S27). A Rs 1.23 cr related-party loan was outstanding at 31 July 2026 (S10). No promoter-owned supplier or customer of material size appears in the sources we could open. On the evidence available the RPTs look routine, but the full RPT schedule in the RHP could not be read directly (see method).

The bigger issue is pay. With effect from 1 April 2025, Vinay Gupta's monthly ceiling rose from Rs 5.40 lakh to Rs 16.00 lakh and Ruchira Gupta's from Rs 4.60 lakh to Rs 14.00 lakh, three times the previous combined level (S7). Actual FY26 pay was Rs 1.985 cr and Rs 1.745 cr, or Rs 3.73 cr together (S7). That is about 9% of FY26 PAT of Rs 41.43 cr (S1), set just before listing.

Not a red flag on its own, but a pre-listing jump in promoter pay, together with insiders selling in the OFS at a WACA of Rs 4.30-14.80 (S1), tells minority shareholders how the family weighs its own interests against outside shareholders' (S7).

items: Credit rating: downgraded in FY22 to CARE BB- with an 'Issuer Not Cooperating' tag for not submitting information (S1, S27, S29). The RHP also admits the company was classified 'Issue not Cooperating' by some agencies after not renewing mandates (S1). CRISIL assigned BBB+/Stable on 2 April 2026 (S20).
Statutory filings: the RHP discloses a history of delayed statutory filings, with adjudication proceedings pending before the Registrar of Companies, Jaipur (S5).

Litigation: no criminal proceedings and no regulatory actions against the company, directors or promoters. The company has filed two material civil cases, and there are four tax cases against it worth Rs 44.62 lakh (S1). Promoters face four tax proceedings worth Rs 224.02 lakh (S1).

Writ petitions against Rajasthan discoms: one challenges a Rs 3.60 cr recovery order from JVVNL based on an Accountant General audit of a project completed in 2019; a Rs 1.09 cr performance guarantee is at risk and the next hearing is on 16 November 2026 (S12). A second, pending since 2021, concerns copper-transformer price variation with AVVNL under DDUGJY after a CAG objection (S6, S12).
Auditor: no reservations, qualifications or adverse remarks except as disclosed in the restated statements (S1).

blocks.text: Overall, governance is adequate but not clean. There is nothing criminal or regulatory against the company. But a rating-agency non-cooperation episode, delayed ROC filings, a pre-listing pay jump and cheap insider transfers all point to a promoter family still adjusting to listed-company discipline (S1, S5, S7, S8).

Vatsalya Gupta is a named promoter with no shareholding, and the RHP states there are no shareholders in the promoter group (S1). The listing will be the first time these promoters face continuous disclosure obligations.

items: Cash conversion: operating cash flow was negative in FY24, FY25 and FY26, adding up to about Rs -89.5 cr against Rs 82.9 cr of PAT (S1). Growth keeps absorbing cash through retention money (Rs 160.02 cr) and receivables (Rs 114.98 cr) (S9).

Customer and policy dependence: 96.87% of revenue comes from government utilities, 100% of the order book is government work, and the top five customers give 96.87% of revenue (S1, S6). Any slowdown after RDSS, or discom payment stress, would hit revenue and cash together.

Project concentration: the five largest projects make up 69.72% of unexecuted work, and one Rajasthan project alone is 24.58% (S6). The RHP admits delays on most projects over the last three years (S1).
Order replenishment: order-book cover has fallen from 2.08x to 1.41x revenue (S1). The company wins only a minority of the tenders it enters, 8 of 28 in FY26 (S6).

blocks.text: These risks feed into one another. A delay on the Sikar or Pugal project (S6) would slow billing. Slower billing means retention money and receivables stay locked up longer (S9), which pushes the company further onto short-term supplier-finance lines (S10). That chain is how a few years of fast P&L growth ended up producing negative operating cash flow (S1).
Negative operating cash flow is the risk that matters most. Everything else, including concentration and tender dependence, shows up through it (S1, S11).

items: Short-term, unsecured funding: 57% of borrowings is channel finance and TReDS from a few fintech and bank discounting platforms (S10). If these lines are pulled, suppliers must be paid in cash.

Guarantee exposure: contingent liabilities of Rs 272.68 cr are about 1.7x FY26 net worth (S5, S1). Audit-driven recoveries after completion, like the Rs 3.60 cr JVVNL demand, can trigger encashment of guarantees (S12).
Governance and ratings history: an FY22 downgrade with an 'Issuer Not Cooperating' tag, and pending ROC adjudication for delayed filings (S1, S5, S27).
Seasonality: the RHP flags seasonal variation in execution and difficulty forecasting project schedules (S1). Half-yearly results after listing may be lumpy.

blocks.text: Several items in the RHP's risk list are generic boilerplate, such as intellectual-property protection (S1), and do not affect the decision. The eight risks above are the ones that decide whether the 35% RoNW (S1) ever becomes free cash for shareholders.

Litigation risk is contained but not zero. The company's writs against Rajasthan discoms (S12) show that utilities can reopen payments years after a project closes, based on audit objections. Retention money and guarantees therefore stay at risk well after completion (S9, S12).

subsections.title: What management has actually committed to

blocks.text: The only quantified forward-looking disclosure we found is the FY27 working-capital plan in the objects section. It projects net working capital rising to Rs 415.97 cr from Rs 255.63 cr, with receivable days improving to 75 and payable days falling to 60 (S9). Growth of that size implies materially higher FY27 revenue, but management gives no explicit revenue or margin guidance in the material we reviewed. We do not infer one.

items: Stated strategies are to use core competencies to grow in distribution EPC, expand into new states, focus on high-value EPC projects and diversify into allied infrastructure sectors (S1).
FY26 milestones management highlights: entry into power transmission and renewable-energy evacuation, and its largest single distribution order, from AVVNL (S14).
Near-term execution depends on Rs 916.55 cr of unexecuted orders at 31 July 2026 (S1). That is about 1.8x FY26 revenue from operations of Rs 503.57 cr (S1).

blocks.text: We found no investor call, earnings guidance or management interview with concrete targets. The outlook rests on the order book and the working-capital plan, not on any stated growth target (S1, S9).

Revenue for FY27 looks reasonably visible from the existing order book (S1). The open question is FY28 onwards. The RDSS sanction window ran from FY22 to FY26 (S26), and the order book's cover of revenue has been falling (S1). The Pugal solar-park evacuation order (S6) suggests renewable-energy transmission could become a second source of orders, but it is too early to rely on that.

The most important thing to track is whether the FY27 working-capital assumptions hold (S9), not the growth rate. If receivable days fall and retention money is released as early RDSS projects close, cash flow could turn positive quickly. If not, the company will be back to borrowing, or raising equity again, within a couple of years (S10, S11).

Two things will show whether the outlook holds: cash flow from operations in the first half-yearly results after listing, and new order announcements, which listed status will now require the company to disclose (S1, S9).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: On 22 September 2026 the company raised Rs 48.26 cr from six anchor investors, allotting 26,08,782 shares at Rs 185, or 30% of the issue (S18, S17). Shine Star Build-Cap, Minerva Ventures Fund and Longthrive Capital VCC (Trendview Capital Fund) each took about 20.72% of the anchor book. Krone Finstock took 17.11%, and Swyom India Alpha and ASAS Global Fund took 10.36% each (S17). No large domestic mutual fund appears among the anchors. The anchor lock-in follows SEBI ICDR rules, but we did not find the specific lock-in end dates in any source we opened.

blocks.caption: Share reservation at the upper band (S17)

blocks.text: This report was written on day 1 (23 September 2026). Tracking sites showed the issue at 0x overall, with retail and NII also 0x, at the time checked (S30). Another source said live subscription data was not yet available (S18). No meaningful category-wise figures exist yet, and QIB and large-HNI bids usually come on the last day.

The unofficial grey-market premium has been small and has moved around: Rs 3 on 21 September (S22), Rs 3-5 over 18-21 September (S14), Rs 7 on the evening of 22 September (S17), and Rs 8 on 23 September (S25), roughly 2-4% over the Rs 185 cap. GMP is unregulated and plays no part in this report's verdict.

method: The full RHP is on the company's site (swastikainfra.com/PDF/IPO/Swastika_RHP.pdf) but could not be read: it is larger than the fetch tool's 10 MB limit and direct download was not permitted. The DRHP link on the company site returned no readable content. The primary document actually read was the SEBI-filed Abridged Prospectus of 17 September 2026 (S1), which summarises the RHP. From it we took segment revenue, top-1/5/10 customer concentration, restated financials and KPIs, cash flows, objects, pre-IPO placement, selling shareholders and their WACA, board, top-10 risk factors and the litigation summary. Deeper RHP detail was cross-checked across several secondary deep-reads of the RHP (S5-S14, S20): order-book composition, the working-capital assessment, borrowing mix, promoter pay and share transfers, litigation, and the FY22 rating and ROC history. The core financials match across S1, S4, S15 and S17. Gaps: (1) supplier names and supplier concentration were not available in any source; (2) the full related-party schedule was not read directly, and the RPT percentages (S27) and peer names (S28) come from WebSearch result snippets of pages that returned 403 when opened, so treat them as less verified; (3) no state-wise revenue split was found; (4) the exact amount for general corporate purposes and issue expenses is not yet fixed (Rs [*] in the RHP); (5) anchor lock-in end dates were not confirmed. Some secondary sources conflict and were resolved in favour of S1: working capital Rs 90 cr, not the DRHP-era Rs 145 cr or one site's Rs 128.09 cr; FY26 revenue from operations Rs 503.57 cr versus total income Rs 505.57 cr. Day-1 subscription was 0x or unavailable at the time of writing. Valuation metrics volunteered by sources (P/E, P/B, peer multiples) were deliberately excluded, as instructed.
